card_text: Submission to the Standing Committee on Health Study on Women’s Health – Women’s Cancers Date: February 12, 2024 Submitted by: Dr Shannon Salvador President-Elect, Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada (GOC) Associate Professor, McGill University Head of Colposcopy, Jewish General Hospital Program Director, McGill Gynecologic Oncology Residency Program A history of gynecologic oncology and the Society of Gynecologic Oncologists of Canada (GOC) Historically, women’s cancers have been orphaned from traditional cancer care models. In the 1970s and 80’s a dedicated group of physicians created the gynecologic oncology sub-specialty to care for women with cancers of the ovary, uterus, cervix, vulva, and placenta. Among all surgical cancer specialties, ours is unique because the care is comprehensive, including diagnosis, surgery, systemic treatments (e.g., chemotherapy), surveillance, and palliative care. Only recently has patient care incorporated other disciplines, such as dedicated medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, palliative care teams and specialized nurses have begun collaborating with gynecologic oncology teams. Due to such historic isolation and separation from the traditional oncology care model, these cancers have long been deemed a “women’s issue.” Funding for clinical care and research has not kept pace with other, more common, cancers, such as colorectal, breast and lung. GOC, a non-profit organization, was created 40 years ago as a forum for medical professionals to highlight issues in women’s cancer care across Canada and help correct the disparity in cancer care access and equity in research funding for new treatments1. Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty National pharmaceutical sovereignty ensures that Canadians have reliable access to highquality medicines and treatments when they need them. This means having a strong domestic manufacturing capacity and integration into key supply chains. Medicines and the systems that produce them sit at the intersection of public health, economic growth and national security. When a country’s pharmaceutical industry is dependent on foreign-owned firms and imported inputs, it may not reflect domestic priorities, leaving the country vulnerable to market forces and supply chain disruptions. Canada relies heavily on global supply chains for access to pharmaceuticals: almost all active pharmaceutical ingredients used in Canada are imported, with a majority from China and India, creating a concentration risk in critical inputs.i Canada also faces persistent and significant drug shortages. A stable supply is necessary to keep costs down, avoid expensive solutions to sudden shocks or emergencies and maintain access for all Canadians. The government should seek to bolster Canada’s biopharma capacity and self-suIiciency through targeted policy action and closer collaboration with industry. Other countries already recognize domestic drug manufacturing as a core component of national security. The United States’ Defence Production Act makes explicit that America views building biopharmaceutical resilience as an important national security priority. Similarly, the European Union’s Critical Medicines Act seeks to modernize and expand its domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. Canada must act to support its own pharmaceutical and biomanufacturing sectors to ensure resiliency. [ORG] submits this brief to the Standing Committee on Health to highlight the importance of sonographers in the Canadian healthcare system and the barriers to internationally trained professionals. Executive Summary: Diagnostic medicine is a vital but often less recognized component of the Canadian healthcare system, which has been increasingly under strain for the last five years. One important aspect of the diagnostic ecosystem in Canada is sonography. Sonography is the practice of using ultrasound as a medical investigation to assess organs, tissues, and blood flow inside the body. Diagnostic medical sonographers perform at least 10 million ultrasound scans in Canada each year. These highly skilled professionals are a vital part of the care economy and consistently enable improved health outcomes for Canadians, from diagnosis through patient care. Sonographers have been bearing the brunt of a medical system under strain, resulting in a shortage of Canadian-trained sonographers who are ready to enter active practice. However, there is a solution to this issue in supporting and funding programs for internationally trained medical professionals to transition into Canadian sonography practice. Current Situation: Sonography is practiced differently around the world. In most countries, sonography is performed by physicians who have the essential skills to become sonographers in Canada, should they wish to do so. With fundamental medical skills in place, most only need to familiarize themselves with Canadian practice norms and standards and acclimate to the Canadian health care system to succeed. card_text: Inter-provincial Barriers to Pediatric Clinical Research Submission to the Sanding Committee on Health October 25, 2022 [ORG] ([ORG]) Submitted by: Thierry Lacaze-Masmonteil, MD, PhD Background Economic, ethical, regulatory and infrastructure considerations associated with the conduct of child health research have limited the number of drug clinical trials conducted with children. Several challenges, more frequently encountered when conducting clinical trials with a pediatric population, have contributed to current gaps in the evidence base on medicines for children. On one hand, many diseases occur less frequently in children and neonates, compared to adults. On the other hand, some diseases only occur in children or have etiology or physiopathology different from the adult population. Other challenges with neonatal or pediatric clinical trials include the frequent lack of age-appropriate and validated clinical endpoints, the paucity of data on normal laboratory values, the need for sensitive assays to minimize blood sampling, and the fact that, while they cannot legally provide consent, children should be informed and have a voice regarding participation. Therefore, in order to engage sufficient participants in a timely fashion and to execute well and appropriately powered studies, pediatric clinical trials often require recruitment and enrollment at multiple sites across multiple jurisdictions. Cancer prevention is far more effective and humane, and less costly for children, families, and society than treatment. While early detection has value, reduction of toxic exposures at homes and school environments should be paramount. We are deeply concerned that the escalating use of wireless devices and infrastructure (cell towers and antennas) intensifies RF-EMR exposures in educational settings. A substantial body of scientific evidence shows RF-EMR can cause biological effects linked to serious health issues, including cancers. [ORG] is an organization that provides health care to people who are homeless or vulnerably housed1. We offer a wide variety of shelter based and supportive housing-based social-determinants of health services for individuals, the vast majority of whom use drugs. Since 2001, we have been leading responses to changes in Ottawa’s unregulated, non-prescribed drugs market including the recent acceleration of changes to what we now call the toxic drug supply. It is important to understand that situation on the ground across Canada is evolving rapidly and our collective response is lagging. While the strategies of a decade ago continue to mitigate some of the harms, that mitigation has become less effective due to changes in the content and potency of this drug supply, the social safety net, brain and drug clearance physiology from aging & repeated use and in the behaviour of some of those most impacted. This is compounded by lack of meaningful investment in services to support chronic pain, substance use and mental health including complex trauma treatment. Submission Brief Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty May 5, 2026 [ORG] Submitted to Standing Committee on Health (HESA) House of Commons Executive Summary The goal of strengthening Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty is widely shared, and strengthening domestic supply and improving patient access is critical to realize this goal. But successful pharmaceutical sovereignty requires a balanced, whole-system approach that includes all aspects of the innovation and pharmaceutical supply sectors. A narrow policy lens that favours domestic biomanufacturing in isolation must carefully consider downstream implications specifically on Canadians; those for whom these policies are being considered. Biomanufacturing is deeply connected with global supply chains, drawing on a complex, globally distributed network of innovators and suppliers, each providing critical components. Any policy that solely prioritizes domestic biomanufacturing, without an equal investment in other aspects of the pharmaceutical supply chain and innovation, can reduce competitive pressure, slow development, constrain supply and ultimately exacerbate the current risk of increased drug shortages as well as increasing costs and barriers to patient access. Pharmaceutical sovereignty is often discussed in terms of manufacturing capacity and upstream supply, but it must ultimately be measured by whether medicines reliably reach patients. True sovereignty is realized at the point of care. While strengthening domestic production and diversifying supply sources are important objectives, they are insufficient on their own if medicines cannot be accessed, substituted, or sustained when the system experiences disruption. I have a Doctor of Philosophy degree in occupational and environmental health from the University of Stirling, in Scotland. In 2004, I retired after thirty-four years with the Government of Canada. In the 1970s, I was part of the organization charged with implementing the Environmental Contaminants Act (1975) and I worked as the Early Warning Coordinator identifying sentinel biological events from exposures to chemicals in the environment. My final years of service were with the International Joint Commission where I specialized in inferring the causal relations between the biological effects observed in fish, wildlife and human populations exposed to persistent toxic chemicals in Great Lakes food webs. Following my retirement from public service, I co-chaired the Halifax Project, an initiative involving 350 cancer scientists from 31 countries, half of whom were focused on the potential role of low-dose, biologically disruptive, common environmental chemicals that might be acting in concert with one another and contributing to various aspects of carcinogenesis.
